markdown_chunks.text:
Design Approach

The absence of circumferential heat flux data to simulate the real behavior of coolant channels is a serious limitation in designing for reliability and robustness. The approach has been to scale available calorimeter (1 dimensional) heat flux data to the appropriate chamber pressure and mixture ratio of interest. other issues that have not properly entered into the design criteria are sensitivity of channel

localized effects on the type of failure mode under consideration, channel flow maldistribution and gas-side wall oxidation. In addition, the important factors influencing the design approach are cycle requirements and design constraints. The former consists of engine mission, thrust, specific impulse, chamber pressure, propellants/mixture ratio, cost, and v weight. The most important design constraint is the limitation on the regenerative coolant pressure drop which is a function of the allowable gas-side wall temperature, pump discharge pressure, v coolant flow direction, coolant passage geometry including a constraint on the number of channels, and flow rate. Chamber

length and diameter, convergence angle, chamber/nozzle attachment location, and nozzle exit area ratio are some of the geometric constraints imposed on the cooling design. Large chambers (i.e. high thrust, low chamber pressure) have been of tubular construction because of weight and flexibility-in-cooling advantages. With the current trend toward higher heat loads

The bulk temperature of the coolant entering the high heat flux region at the throat was seen to strongly influence the

overall pressure drop. Since a mixer would be required for coolant flows less than

The design criteria called for sizing the channels under a so called hot channel scenario. Wall blanching and surface roughening results from the incompatability between wall and environment. For every material, the surface oxidation rate (i.e wall blanching and surface roughening) is a

and by adding film cooling as necessary to iachieve a desired maximum wall temperature based on life cycle requirements. Fundamental to arriving at an optimum chamber cooling system is integrated analysis which consists of taking into account all important effects (i.e. system/component) in the final design.

The main deficiency in the design criteria of Table 1 was in sizing the hot channel. In reality, the hot channel should represent a worst case scenario where there is no dependence on fuel film cooling, and local hot spots exist along the walls of this channel due to injector streaking effects. In addition, the Coolant flow through the hot channel has been reduced due to an increase in flow resistance. In normal operating conditions, a channel will benefit from fuel film cooling and not be exposed to streaks or any causes for coolant flow maldistribution. The performance of the nominal channel will represent the average coolant exit conditions. For chamber survivability, however, the channels are designed to accommodate the hot walls.

Based on the above rationale, a chamber design criteria has recently been

formulated by Aerojet that includes sizing the channels according to new conditions defined under the "hot channel" scenario but whose performance characteristics are based on an improved "nominal channel" scenario. For a pre-established chamber length and diameter based on weight/volume and combustion stability considerations, channel design is performed with barrier cooling as needed to avoid wall blanching. with the aid of recent Aerojet calorimeter measurements (Fall, 1990) which included segmented axial circuits in the chamber section for limited circumferential data, the injector streaking effect was taken

into account by a 10% increase in chamber heat flux. Flow maldistribution due to the combined effects of channel inlet manifold, manufacturing tolerance, and streaking (i .e. increased flow resistance) is accounted for by reducing the actual flow through the channel by 10%. The channels are designed with an over-sized wall (i.e. thicker than nominal) for heat transfer but with an under-sized wall (i.e. thinner than nominal) for strength. With a thicker wall, the heat transfer conductance is

reduced, and with a thinner wall, the

channel is designed to withstand the pressure differential across the wall. A maximum channel depth to width ratio of seven is allowed based on current chamber manufacturing techniques. The allowable design gas-side wall temperature is set to a relatively high value based on sensitivity of the material yield strength. Table 2 summarizes the "hot channel" design criteria. With a channel profile at hand,

Chamber cooling designs for the GG cycle were performed with the advanced philosophy summarized in Table 2 . These results were then compared with the cooling designs obtained based on the former design philosophy (Table 1) in order to assess the relative impact on the performance of the system. Besides the advantage of designing to a maximum wall temperature, the advanced chamber desisn criteria offers a comoromise between pump power requirement and engine specific impulse.

Former Design Philosophy

The percent flow through the jacket at a given barrier mixture ratio (MRb) was varied and the resulting pressure drop was obtained. For a cost efficient fabrication process, however, it was necessary to specify the number of channels in the u design. Thus, at each flow rate, the channel geometry was optimized to produce the same number of channels at minimum pressure drop. The minimum number of channels required was obtained by a sensitivity analysis at the given engine operating conditions as depicted in Figure 2 . Since the amount of flow through the jacket was unknown at this point, full flow

(i.e. 100%) was considered. The selected range for barrier mixture ratio conformed to the wall mixture ratio limitation. The results according to Figure 2 indicated that based on Mach number limitation, 325 channels would be the minimum number obtainable and that the number of channels would become insensitive to coolant pressure drop and Mach number above 4 2 5 . Thus, parametric studies were performed to obtain the optimum flow split by selecting 372 channels at the first iteration. Figure 3 shows the flow split at each barrier mixture ratio which satisfies the design criteria. The results indicate the relation between component and system performance. Every pressure drop curve is associated with a curve for maximum Mach number at a given barrier mixture ratio.
